explanation: A demand for something that is wanted for what it produces, not for itself. Health care is wanted because it helps produce health.
How strongly the quantity demanded reacts to a change in price: the % change in quantity divided by the % change in price.
When being insured changes behaviour: people use more care, or take less care of their health, because insurance lowers the price they face.
Making the insured person pay part of the cost of care, for example through deductibles, copayments or coinsurance.
When people know more about their own health risk than the insurer, high-risk people are more likely to buy insurance. This can push premiums up and drive low-risk people out.
The application of economic reasoning to choices, incentives and the allocation of scarce resources related to health and healthcare.
Resources spent on healthcare. It can be compared across countries as a level, per person, or as a share of GDP.
The value of the best alternative that must be given up when a choice is made.
Studying the effect of one additional unit of an activity, input or resource rather than focusing only on totals or averages.
A situation in which one party has better or more relevant information than another, such as a physician knowing more about diagnosis and treatment than a patient.
Uncertainty about future health, when care will be needed, which treatment will be appropriate, what it will cost and what outcome will follow.
A cost or benefit created by an action that affects people other than the person making the decision.
Using available resources so that avoidable waste is reduced and the greatest feasible value can be produced.
Fairness in how resources, opportunities, access or outcomes are distributed across people or groups.
Financing healthcare through a third party such as an insurer or government instead of relying only on direct payment at the point of use.
A payment made directly by a patient for healthcare rather than being fully financed by an insurer or government.
A framework linking the three central actors in healthcare: patient, provider and insurer/government.
A relationship showing how much of a good or service consumers are willing and able to buy at each price, holding other determinants constant.
The maximum amount a buyer is willing to pay for a good or service, used as a measure of how much the buyer values it.
The buyer's willingness to pay minus the amount actually paid.
A midpoint-based elasticity measure between two price-quantity points, useful for comparing responsiveness without depending on the units used.
A study that randomly assigns participants to different conditions so the groups are comparable on average before treatment.
The monetary price of care plus other costs borne by the patient, including travel costs and the opportunity cost of time.
An insurance payment that contributes a fixed amount for a covered service, leaving the patient responsible for the remaining price.
The fraction of the healthcare bill paid by the patient, with the insurer paying the rest.
A fixed amount paid by the patient each time a covered healthcare service is used.
An amount the patient pays toward medical bills before insurance reimbursement begins.
